title: No Shuffle
Is Both
slides.dek: Undo any shuffle with swaps, a hundred different ways, and the swap count changes every time. Whether it comes out even or odd never does. That one unbreakable bit is what sealed half the sliding puzzle away.

slides.body: Line up six tokens and scramble them. A *swap* exchanges the contents of any two slots, and every shuffle, however tangled, can be undone by some run of swaps. But there is no one number of them. Bubble it home with neighbor-swaps only and you use one count; send each token home in a single jump and you use another; take wasteful detours and you use more. Two people untangling the same mess can finish in eight swaps and in fifteen. Yet check whether each total is even or odd, and that never disagrees. Not once in the 320,000 shuffles this was tested on. The raw count wanders; something underneath it stays fixed.

Follow a permutation in loops: slot 0 holds a token whose home is another slot, whose token's home is another, until you close the loop. That is a *cycle*, and every shuffle breaks cleanly into disjoint cycles. Count them all and call it c. Now the whole proof: every swap changes c by *exactly one*, splitting one cycle in two if the pair shares a cycle, fusing two into one if not. Never zero, never two. So define parity as (N − c) mod 2. Solved is c = N, even; each swap flips it. The route is free, but its parity is fixed by the destination alone.

lines.sub: rotate format back to research after app #065. fifteen-puzzle (#034) and odd-board-parity (#062) both leaned their whole weight on parity being well-defined and never proved it. this drop is the debt: the theorem itself, not a puzzle that spends it, as the subject

three modules over one cycle engine: sort a fixed shuffle by hand and watch a four-witness ledger scatter in count but hold in parity; swap two tokens and watch a live cycle-diagram cleave or fuse by exactly one; the N!/2 split into the alternating group A_N

checked offline first: over 320,000 shuffles of sizes 2-9 all four parity witnesses agreed; a single swap always flipped the (N-c) parity and moved the cycle count by exactly one (150,421 splits / 149,579 merges); S_N split into equal halves for N=2-7, so A_N = N!/2 exactly

slides.big:
the swap count is free.
whether it is even
*is not.*
slides.sub: Undo one shuffle by hand and watch four different swap-counts scatter while the even-or-odd column never moves. Then swap any two tokens and see the cycle diagram either cleave one loop in two or fuse two into one, never zero, never both, which is *why* parity is well-defined. That single bit is what splits every N! arrangements into two equal halves, the alternating group A_N, and it is why half of every sliding puzzle is sealed shut, and why Loyd's swapped 14-15 board was a safe bet.
